newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian opposition on attack, Yeltsin out of sight.
newsitem.headline: Russian opposition on attack, Yeltsin out of sight.

text.p: Russia's domestic phoney war between Boris Yeltsin and the communists who dominate parliament seems set to go on as the rhetoric and constitutional confusion intensify and the convalescent president stays out of sight.
Yeltsin's antagonists on Wednesday launched their biggest offensive since their defeat in last July's presidential election.

The State Duma lower house of parliament approved "in principle" a resolution that Yeltsin, who dropped from view with heart trouble after his reelection and is now recovering from pneumonia, be removed from office on health grounds.
The vote, however, was not conclusive. And in any case, the Duma's own lawyers ruled the motion legally void.
The presidential press service said Yeltsin visited his Kremlin office on Wednesday, just two days after leaving hospital, and met Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.
But the Russian public has not seen a single picture of Yeltsin since he went down with pneumonia on January 6.

Chief Kremlin doctor Sergei Mironov said on Tuesday that Yeltsin still planned to fly to The Hague on February 3, two days after his 66th birthday. The doctor said on Wednesday it would be two or three weeks from now before he recovered fully.

Mironov said Yeltsin's condition was "quite satisfactory" but admitted he was "quick to tire" and did not "feel very comfortable". He also chided the president for being in too great a hurry to prove he was back in the driving seat.
Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov said Yeltsin should appear before the Duma to explain. But it was left to chief spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky to launch the counterblast to parliament.

Asked why the president himself had not reacted to the vote, Yastrzhembsky was quoted by Interfax news agency as saying: "You can't compare the president, a superheavyweight fighter, with boxers who box at bantam or flyweight."
"It's not up to the president to answer every whine, to answer every sob and every criticism that comes from the opposition benches."
Opposition lawmakers did not spare Yeltsin, in return.

Viktor Ilyukhin, the communist who proposed the motion calling for new elections, told the chamber Kremlin officials were creating an illusion that the president was running the country. He renewed charges that Yeltsin drank heavily.
"Either we agree to Russia's collapse or try to do something about it," Ilyukhin said.
Many government supporters boycotted the debate and leading liberal Grigory Yavlinsky, who campaigned against Yeltsin last year, said it was like a debate in a lunatic asylum.

Some opposition legislators also complained the motion to oust Yeltsin was too extreme, particularly in view of the lack of constitutional grounds for parliament to dismiss the president. Ilyukhin recommended they discuss it with their constituents before returning for a final vote on it next month.
After a period of confusion, during which the speaker said the chamber had changed its mind and thrown out the motion, the Duma press service said the deputies postponed a final decision.
It is not clear just what the Duma will do next.

Yeltsin's representative to the lower house, Alexander Kotenkov, warned that adopting such a resolution could even lead to civil war -- raising the spectre of 1993, when Yeltsin sent tanks against the hostile Soviet-era Russian parliament.
One pro-government deputy said the president might be wise to dissolve parliament -- although the constitutional provisions for doing so are, in theory, extremely limited.

Many opposition leaders seem unwilling to push the conflict to the limits, however. A leading communist told Reuters: "It doesn't matter what happens to this resolution. What matters is that we're now having a debate on who should run the country."
